title: MemoryDecay: Biologically-Inspired Forgetting Mechanisms for Agentic Memory Systems
description: Problem: Current agentic memory systems like A-MEM treat all memories as equally persistent, causing retrieval degradation as memory networks grow unbounded. Real agents accumulating months of experience face noise from outdated, contradicted, or low-utility memories that pollute retrieval and reasoning. Biological memory selectively forgets through decay and consolidation—a principle absent from LLM memory systems. Proposed Method: We introduce MemoryDecay, extending A-MEM's Zettelkasten-inspired architecture with three biologically-grounded mechanisms: (1) Temporal decay scoring that exponentially reduces memory salience based on recency and access frequency, modeled after Ebbinghaus forgetting curves; (2) Contradiction-triggered pruning where newly integrated memories that semantically conflict with existing nodes trigger agent-driven evaluation to archive or delete stale entries; (3) Consolidation cycles that periodically merge clusters of highly-linked, thematically similar memories into compressed 'schema' nodes, reducing network density while preserving core knowledge. Decay parameters are dynamically adjusted per memory based on task-relevance signals. Experiments: We evaluate on LongMemEval and LoCoMo benchmarks extending evaluation horizons to 10k+ interactions, measuring retrieval precision, reasoning accuracy, and memory network size over time. Ablations isolate each decay component. Comparisons include A-MEM, MemGPT, and Zep. We hypothesize 15%+ precision improvement at scale while reducing active memory nodes by 40%.

title: MemForget: Selective Memory Decay and Privacy-Preserving Forgetting in Agentic Memory Systems
description:
Problem: Current agentic memory systems like A-MEM focus exclusively on memory acquisition and organization, but neglect a critical capability: strategic forgetting. In real-world deployments, LLM agents accumulate stale, contradictory, or privacy-sensitive memories that degrade performance over time and create compliance risks (e.g., GDPR right-to-erasure). There is no principled mechanism for deciding what to forget, when to forget it, and how forgetting should propagate through interconnected memory networks.

Proposed Method: We introduce MemForget, a decay-aware agentic memory system built on A-MEM's Zettelkasten-inspired architecture. We augment each memory note with temporal relevance scores and privacy sensitivity tags. A forgetting agent periodically evaluates memories using three criteria: (1) recency-weighted access frequency, (2) semantic redundancy with newer memories, and (3) explicit deletion requests. Crucially, when a memory is flagged for removal, a graph-propagation algorithm re-evaluates and updates all linked notes to preserve network coherence, analogous to A-MEM's memory evolution but in reverse.

Planned Experiments: We evaluate on longitudinal QA benchmarks (LoCoMo, StreamingQA) measuring accuracy on recent vs. stale facts, compliance benchmarks testing successful erasure without collateral accuracy loss, and ablations comparing decay strategies (time-based, usage-based, hybrid). We compare against A-MEM and MemGPT baselines across three LLM backbones.

title: MemoryForge: Continual Learning Through Conflict-Aware Memory Consolidation in LLM Agents

A confidence-weighted retrieval mechanism then surfaces memories appropriate to the current context. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) longitudinal user preference tracking benchmarks where preferences evolve, (2) factual knowledge update tasks (e.g., changing world facts), and (3) multi-session dialogue consistency. Baselines include A-MEM, MemGPT, and Reflexion. Metrics include contradiction rate, task accuracy over time, and memory precision/recall.

Problem: Current agentic memory systems like A-MEM treat all memories equally regardless of age or access frequency, leading to retrieval noise as memory networks grow large over extended deployments. Human memory research shows that strategic forgetting via decay curves (Ebbinghaus) improves recall efficiency and reduces interference. No existing LLM memory system incorporates principled temporal decay into dynamic memory networks.

Proposed Method: We augment the A-MEM architecture with a biologically-inspired forgetting mechanism. Each memory note receives a dynamic salience score combining recency (exponential decay), access frequency (spaced-repetition reinforcement), and structural centrality (degree in the memory graph). During retrieval, low-salience memories are deprioritized but not deleted—instead compressed into abstract 'consolidated' nodes via LLM-driven summarization, merging related decayed memories into higher-level concepts. Memory links inherit and propagate salience scores, enabling cascade reinforcement when connected memories are accessed.

Experiments: (1) Long-horizon task benchmarks (LongMemEval, LoCoMo) measuring retrieval precision as memory count scales from 100 to 10,000 notes. (2) Ablations comparing no-decay, fixed-decay, and adaptive-decay variants. (3) Memory efficiency metrics: storage size vs. task performance trade-offs. (4) Comparison against A-MEM, MemGPT, and Mem0 baselines across six LLM backbones. We expect 15-20% improvement in retrieval precision at scale with 40% reduction in active memory footprint.
